talk: Every choice has a price you don't see on the invoice: the best thing you gave up to make it. That's opportunity cost. A good decision has to beat the next best option, not just zero.

terms.meaning: The value of the best option you didn't choose.
Picking one thing means giving up another.
The choice you'd make if this one weren't on the table.

questions.prompt: The pitch is free on Saturday. A concert promoter will pay $60,000 to hire it. A friendly match would bring in $40,000 of profit. What's the opportunity cost of playing the friendly?
questions.hint: What do you give up by playing?
working: Playing the friendly means saying no to the concert.
The best thing you give up is the concert's $60,000.
$40,000 - $60,000 = -$20,000. The friendly leaves you $20,000 worse off.
whyNot: $60,000 - $40,000 = $20,000 is how much better the concert is. The opportunity cost is the whole $60,000 you give up.
$40,000 is what the friendly earns, not what it costs you.
$60,000 + $40,000 = $100,000 adds both options together. You can only pick one.

questions.prompt: Your best coach could run the academy, worth $120,000 a year to the club, or coach the first team's set pieces, worth $90,000. There's only time for one. If the coach takes set pieces, what's the opportunity cost?
questions.hint: Opportunity cost is the value of the job not chosen.
working: Choosing set pieces means giving up the academy.
The academy is worth $120,000, so that's the opportunity cost.
$90,000 - $120,000 = -$30,000. Set pieces is the worse choice by $30,000.
whyNot: $120,000 - $90,000 = $30,000 is the gap between the two jobs. The opportunity cost is the full value of the job given up.
$90,000 is what set pieces are worth. That's the job being done, not the one given up.
$120,000 + $90,000 = $210,000 assumes the coach can do both. There's time for one.

questions.prompt: You have $1M spare. Option A: new hospitality boxes earning $150,000 a year. Option B: pay off a loan that charges 8% interest a year. How much more a year do the boxes earn than paying off the loan?
questions.hint: Paying off the loan saves you interest. How much?
working: Paying off the loan saves $1M x 8% = $80,000 a year in interest.
$150,000 - $80,000 = $70,000 more a year from the boxes.
The $80,000 is the opportunity cost of building the boxes. The boxes still win.
whyNot: $80,000 is the interest you'd save by paying off the loan. Compare it with the boxes' $150,000.
$150,000 is what the boxes earn, but spending the $1M on them means not saving $80,000 of interest.

takeaway: Every yes is a no to something else. Count what you give up.
